transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith. Welcome in—what brings you here today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Thanks. Um, I guess I came in because... well, it's mostly my work. I teach high school, secondary school history, which is usually great. Sophomores are actually a really fun age because they're just starting to argue about politics and stuff, though half the time they're just repeating something they heard on a podcast or TikTok, and you have to sort of gently walk them back to actual historical sources... which is a whole thing on its own. 

But, um, anyway, the main reason I'm here is that I'll sit down at my desk with a stack of their essays, or like a new curriculum document, fully intending to just get to work and power through it. And then... I don't know, maybe ten minutes later, I'll realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page the whole time. My brain is off thinking about three completely different things—like if I remembered to take the recycling out, or what I need to get at the grocery store—and I'm barely taking in a single word of what's right in front of me. It's just getting really frustrating.
Has this kind of trouble concentrating been a pattern for you going back to childhood or your school years, or is this something that started more recently?

Yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing. It goes way back. Like, even in primary school, my report cards always said stuff like "bright but careless" or "doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised." And my parents were constantly finding these crumpled-up worksheets at the bottom of my backpack that I just completely forgot to turn in. 

Speaking of backpacks, they really don't make them like they used to, do they? I had this one JanSport bag that lasted me from like third grade all the way into high school. It was that really loud neon green color—which was huge back then, you know? Now I look at my students and they're carrying these tiny little designer bags that can barely fit a single notebook. I mean, I know most of their curriculum is on Chromebooks now, which honestly is a whole other nightmare because the district's Wi-Fi is always going down right in the middle of my lectures and they all just immediately pull out their phones... but anyway, wait. What were we talking about? Oh, right, my childhood. Yeah, the crumpled worksheets and the report card comments were a constant battle.
Aside from the concentration issues, do you often feel restless, fidgety, or have a hard time sitting still—like needing to get up and move around, or feeling internally 'keyed up'?

No, not really. I mean, I don't feel like I have to jump up and run laps around the room or anything. I can sit through a faculty meeting just fine. Well, physically sit there, anyway. Though those meetings are getting ridiculous. Last week our principal spent forty-five minutes talking about the new parking lot policies because apparently some parents have been using the staff spots for drop-off. Which, okay, I get it, it's annoying, but did we really need a PowerPoint presentation with satellite images of the school to explain where the painted lines are? And of course, Mr. Henderson—he teaches chemistry—had to chime in with a whole speech about traffic flow dynamics. He always does that. He thinks because he teaches science he’s an expert on civil engineering. It’s like, Jim, just park your Subaru and come inside. But yeah, no, I don't feel restless or keyed up. I just sit there and space out.
Do you notice similar difficulties with concentration, organization, or forgetfulness in other parts of your life outside of work—like managing household tasks, bills, or personal errands?

Yeah, it’s definitely not just at school. I forget ordinary responsibilities at home way more than I want to admit. Like, just the other day, my wife asked me to pick up something on the way home from work. I think it was oat milk? Which, by the way, have you noticed that the milk aisle is completely out of control now? It used to just be regular milk, maybe soy if you were at a health food store. Now there's oat, almond, cashew, macadamia... how do you even milk a macadamia nut? And the packaging is all so similar. I actually bought the vanilla-flavored oat milk by mistake a few weeks ago, and let me tell you, vanilla oat milk in a savory pasta dish is an absolute disaster. We ended up having to order takeout from this Thai place down the street. Their Pad Thai is usually amazing, but lately, they've been really skimping on the peanuts, which is the best part, honestly. If you're going to charge sixteen dollars for noodles, I feel like you can afford a handful of peanuts, you know? 

Wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, outside of work. Yeah. So I forget errands like that all the time. And bills, too. I always tell myself I'll just log on and pay them real quick, but then I get distracted by something else, and the next thing I know, I'm getting a late notice in the mail. Or I'll completely forget to reply to a parent email that I opened on my phone while I was eating breakfast. The intention is there, it just completely slips my mind.

Have you ever gone through a period—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually energetic, needed much less sleep than normal, or had racing thoughts that made it hard to focus on one thing?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm definitely not someone who can get by on just a few hours of sleep. If I don't get at least seven hours, I am completely useless the next day. Especially with first period starting at 7:45 AM. Who decided teenagers should be learning algebra before the sun is fully up? It's ridiculous. I've been reading about how their circadian rhythms are naturally shifted later, so they're basically sleepwalking through my class. 

Actually, I tried to bring this up at the last school board meeting. I had this whole article printed out from a sleep journal, but the board president—this guy who owns a chain of car washes in town—just kept talking about how pushing start times back would ruin the bus schedules. Like, okay, I get logistics are hard, but isn't the point of a school to actually educate kids when their brains are awake? And speaking of the buses, the exhaust from the older models they run is just awful. When I'm on morning duty out front, you can practically taste the diesel in the air. I had to buy this special air purifier for my classroom just to clear it out, which wasn't cheap, let me tell you. I got it on Amazon, though, so at least it came in two days. But then the delivery driver left it at the wrong door, and it sat out in the rain... 

Wait, sorry. Did I even answer your question? You were asking about sleep, right? Yeah, no, I've never had a time where I felt super energetic or didn't need sleep. I'm usually pretty exhausted by the end of the day.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports chronic, pervasive inattention (losing focus mid-task, forgetting assignments, missing deadlines, difficulty sustaining attention on paperwork/emails/bills) present since primary school, documented by teacher/parent reports ('bright but careless,' incomplete work). Symptoms occur across multiple settings (work and home), causing functional impairment (late bill payments, unanswered parent emails, workplace inefficiency). Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms are explicitly denied (no restlessness, able to sit through meetings). No evidence of manic/hypomanic episodes, mood disorder, or psychotic symptoms. The clinical picture is consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, meeting ICD-10 criteria for F90.0 (Disturbance of Activity and Attention), which encompasses ADHD with attention deficits as the core feature even without prominent hyperactivity, given childhood onset and cross-situational impairment.
